_note: ulthar :: THE single config file. Lives at the skill root (<skill>/config.json), is deployed to ~/.claude/hooks/config.json by install.py, and is the ONLY policy source the Python hook runtime loads. dispatch-map.json and references/viewport-matrix.json are absorbed here and deleted. references/viewport-matrix.md survives as the human doc and points here. Comments use _note keys. Every regex is a Python `re` pattern (inline flags at pattern start only).

regex._note: The plugin layer for policy. ULTHAR ships the mechanism (this section, plus lib/ctx.py:merge_overlays) and universal rules (everything else in this file); WHOSE rules an individual json path holds comes from OUTSIDE ulthar, via the two files named below. Consumed once per dispatch, in dispatch.py's main(), immediately after load_config() and inside its OWN try/except -- a bad overlay is treated exactly like a bad config.json (BLOCK, exit 2, logged to logging.config_error_log, never a silent per-guard fail-open), but it gets its own recovery text (dispatch.infra_recovery.overlay), because 'redeploy the master' is the wrong instruction for a file that is neither under hooks/ nor in git. THE MODEL (owner decision, 2026-09-06): an overlay may ADD rules at the rule paths listed in `project_allowed_paths` and may DISABLE named ones there explicitly, by id (see `_note_disable`). Project configuration takes precedence over personal configuration -- as it does for .editorconfig, linter configs and CI settings -- so a project that switches a guard's rule off on purpose is stating its own policy, and that is not this tool's business. What an overlay may NOT do is weaken anything by ACCIDENT or INVISIBLY, and that takes TWO steps rather than one: (1) a structurally broken entry is refused at MERGE TIME wherever the merge can derive the shape -- declared lists, sections, and (round 4) an undeclared list the user layer replaces wholesale; (2) whatever step 1 cannot see, the dispatcher catches by its consequence -- while ANY overlay is merged, a guard that RAISES blocks and names the overlay file instead of being turned into ALLOW by the fail-open, which is what used to silently remove EVERY rule that guard enforced. Step 1 alone was incomplete four review rounds running; step 2 is the one that does not depend on having anticipated the shape; a `disable` that matches no rule is refused rather than quietly switching nothing off; and a project overlay that disables anything is logged and stated once per session (dispatch.py:_overlay_disable_notice). An overlay that silently degraded to 'ignored' on error would be exactly the hollowing-out this project exists to remove -- a rule nobody can see is gone.

text._note: Matched against command text, brief text, tool names, process command lines, branch names. ALWAYS IGNORECASE — reproduces PowerShell on every platform, and this is platform-independent policy.

path._note: Matched against FILESYSTEM PATHS. IGNORECASE only when ctx.is_windows. A blanket IGNORECASE here would be a LOOSENING on POSIX: `rm -rf /home/x/Dist` would be treated as the disposable `dist/` and slip past the exact rule that protects untracked owner files. POSIX is a new target platform, so there is no existing behaviour to preserve there.

regex._note_ascii: re.ASCII is NOT used and must not be added. .NET regex (PowerShell) treats \w, \b and \s as Unicode-aware by default, and so does Python re on str patterns; adding re.ASCII would DIVERGE from the masters, notably around the Japanese alternatives in the brief-gate patterns.
regex._note_compile_scope: Patterns are compiled lazily PER GUARD, not once globally: a malformed pattern in design_cases must affect ONLY brief_gate, never take tool_discipline or git_discipline down with it. dispatch.py compiles the pattern set a guard declares immediately before calling it. CORRECTION (2026-09-05): this note used to say the affected guard 'fails open and logs'. It does not, and never did in the Python runtime — a pattern that will not compile is an INFRASTRUCTURE failure, not guard logic, so dispatch.py `_run_guard` catches PatternCompileError separately from a guard's own runtime exception and BLOCKS (exit 2) with an actionable message plus one logging.config_error_log line naming the offending JSON path. Only a guard's runtime exception fails open (I-3). When a PROJECT overlay supplied the pattern the block is attributed to that overlay's file instead of to config.json, because redeploying never touches an overlay (see overlays._note_project_allowed_paths, mechanism 3). The per-guard lazy compilation is unchanged by this correction: one guard's uncompilable pattern is never compiled on another guard's behalf, so it cannot make an unrelated guard raise.
regex._note_kind_authority: R-a. THIS LIST IS THE ONLY AUTHORITY for whether a pattern is path-kind or text-kind. A guard MUST NOT infer the kind from the field's name, its section, or what the value looks like. The names are actively misleading in both directions: `path_token_pattern` is kind 'path' but `push_split_pattern` is 'text'; `dev_processes.pattern` matches command lines (text) while `skill_anchor.name_reject_pattern` matches a path fragment. Inferring would silently give a path pattern IGNORECASE on POSIX — reopening N-1 through a different door.
regex._note_sentinel: R-b. `sentinel` marks a literal value at that path which is NOT a regex and must NEVER be compiled. Two paths carry one, both with sentinel '*': dispatch.events.*[].tools and brief_rules.kinds[].match. '*' means 'match anything' and is checked by identity BEFORE any compile attempt. This matters because re.compile('*') RAISES (nothing to repeat) — and under per-guard fail-open that exception would disable the whole guard: for brief_rules.kinds[].match it would take out the creator-kind classifier, so brief_gate would stop classifying creator briefs entirely and every creator gate would go silent. A sentinel check that is skipped fails loudly in tests and silently in production.
regex._note_pattern_fields: THE authoritative enumeration of every regex location in this file, by JSON path. Nothing else here is compiled as a regex. `sentinel` names a literal value at that path that is NOT a regex and is never compiled ('*' = match anything). `template: true` means the value carries a {ref} placeholder substituted (re.escape'd) before compiling. Classification and opt-out are BY JSON PATH, not by id, because most patterns have no id. tests/test_contract.py asserts this list and the file agree in BOTH directions: every path listed here resolves, and every regex-bearing string in the file is listed here.

named_alternations._note: N-4 (found by an internal pre-promotion config probe's substring duplication check, not by review). THE single home for an alternation used by more than one consumer. `Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit` previously appeared THREE times — dispatch.events routing, commander.tools and skill_anchor.write_edit_tools — so adding a fourth edit-style tool meant three separate edits, and missing one would silently leave that tool routed but unguarded (or guarded but unrouted). Consumers reference an entry by name via a `*_named` key and apply their own anchoring: the dispatcher wraps as ^(...)$, and commander/skill_anchor do the same.
named_alternations._note_twin_rule: A `*_named` key and its literal twin must NEVER both be present at the same site (e.g. both `tools` and `tools_named` on one routing rule). This is enforced by tests/test_contract.py, not left to a note — a site carrying both would have two homes again, which is the exact condition N-4 removed, and whichever one the implementation happened to read would be arbitrary.
named_alternations._note_dangling_reference: A `*_named` value that does not resolve to a key of named_alternations is a HARD CONFIG ERROR, never a silent skip. Resolution happens once at config load, before per-guard compilation. Behaviour on a dangling name, stated because the failure is asymmetric and quiet: for a ROUTING rule (dispatch.events[].tools_named) the dispatcher must NOT skip the rule — skipping it silently unroutes deploy, commander and skill_anchor for every Write/Edit call, which is the mirror image of the hole F-21 was about and would leave the main chain able to author deliverables unchecked. Instead the load fails, one logging.config_error_log line names the dangling key, and install.py refuses to deploy (logging.refuse_deploy_on_invalid_config). At runtime, if a deployed config somehow carries one, the affected guard yields ALLOW and logs — but the routing rule itself is treated as a load failure, so the whole config is rejected rather than partially applied.

regex._note_non_pattern_fields: Paths whose key NAME looks regex-ish but whose VALUE is a literal or an enum, never compiled. Declared explicitly so tests/test_contract.py's reverse check ('every regex-bearing string is listed in pattern_fields') is deterministic instead of relying on a name heuristic that would flag these five. redirect_noise_strips/quote_strip_patterns element [0] IS a pattern and is declared; element [1] is the replacement string. ok_marker_match and match_target are enums; comment_prefix ('#'), truncation_suffix and grants.claim_suffix ('.claim', a file-name suffix used with str.endswith and str concatenation, never compiled) are literal text.
regex._note_string_compare_casefold: PowerShell -eq / -contains are case-insensitive, so these ported string compares use str.casefold() on both sides. Path EQUALITY compares (pm-delete-allow) are deliberately excluded: they go through lib/paths.norm_for_compare, which applies os.path.normcase — case-folding on Windows, exact on POSIX.

single_home_rule: _note: every value has EXACTLY ONE key in this file. `paths` holds only cross-cutting paths (used by lib/ or by more than one guard); a path used by exactly one guard lives in that guard's section. `thresholds` holds only cross-cutting numbers; every other number lives in its guard's section. Do not re-introduce a mirror key — a duplicated value that one consumer reads and the owner edits the other of is precisely the hollowing-out this refactor removes.

paths._note: CROSS-CUTTING paths only (used by lib/ or by more than one guard). Single-guard paths live in that guard's section — see single_home_rule. paths._note_deploy_dir_removed: PE-19. `paths.deploy_dir` (previously '~/.claude/hooks' here) was a fifth decorative key: dispatch.py derives its deploy dir from its OWN file location (`config_path.parent` in main()), and install.py derives it the same way (or from --deploy-dir) -- neither ever reads cfg['paths']['deploy_dir'], and grep confirms no other guard/test does either. ctx.deploy_dir (an attribute other guards DO read) is a Ctx field built.py passes to build_ctx, unrelated to this config key sharing its name. paths._note_normalisation: S-9. Filed at the `paths` section level because it governs lib/paths.norm_for_compare, which is used for path EQUALITY compares (pm-delete-allow) — NOT for exempt_patterns, which is regex-matched and never passes through it. (Round 2 misfiled this note inside exempt_patterns, where it described a function that key never calls.) M-9(a), PARITY: normalisation is LEXICAL ONLY — os.path.normpath semantics. Do NOT use Path.resolve(): it follows symlinks, junctions and NTFS reparse points, whereas .NET's [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath (what every master uses) is purely lexical and touches the filesystem not at all. Lexical also means it works on paths that do not exist, which Rule 3 needs when judging a delete target that is about to be removed. Both directions of the junction consequence are recorded in CONTRACT.md F-19.
paths._note_python_exe: Empty means 'resolve from the running interpreter' (lib/paths.resolve_python_exe() falls back to sys.executable) — the correct default for a cloned copy of this skill, which has no reason to know any one machine's interpreter path. Setting this to an absolute path PINS a specific interpreter; that pin is what `install.py --register-settings` writes verbatim into settings.json (and re-verifies matches). A machine-specific pin belongs in the owner's user overlay (paths.python_exe under ~/.claude/ulthar-overlay.json), never in this shipped file -- do not delete this key even when empty; an explicit empty value with this note is discoverable, a missing key is not.

exempt_patterns._note: Coordination paths that are never deliverables. ONE list; consumed by guards.commander AND guards.skill_anchor (these two were byte-identical duplicates in commander-guard.ps1 and skill-anchor.ps1). Stored as forward-slash regex fragments. MATCHING: lib/paths.to_posix() only (separator conversion, NO normcase), then re.search with the flags for kind 'path' — IGNORECASE on Windows, NONE on POSIX (see regex.kinds.path). normcase is NOT applied here because it would lowercase the candidate on Windows and stop '/Temp/claude/' and '/HANDOFF' from ever matching; normcase is for EQUALITY compares only (pm-delete-allow). Do NOT add an inline (?i) to any entry in this list — it would override the per-platform flag and reintroduce the POSIX case-insensitivity bug (N-1).

thresholds._note: CROSS-CUTTING numbers only. Every per-guard number lives in that guard's section (skill_anchor.max_chars, brief_rules.detect.min_length, brief_rules gate6.min_age_sec, artifact_dirs.grace_minutes/max_named, dev_processes.max_listed/cmdline_truncate, git_policy.pr_state.limit) — see single_home_rule.
thresholds._note_subprocess_timeouts: NEW, and deliberately SPLIT. pr-state-guard.ps1's header claims 'the gh call is bounded to a few seconds' but no timeout exists in the code; same for `git rev-parse`. A single shared budget would be wrong in both directions: LOCAL calls (`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`) complete in milliseconds, so a generous shared value lets a wedged local git stall the tool call, while a tight shared value makes a merely-slow NETWORK call (`gh pr list`) time out and silently skip the PR-state check. ctx.run_cmd therefore takes the kind explicitly: local=5s for git plumbing, remote=20s for gh. Both fail open (allow) on timeout. LOGGING OWNERSHIP (contract addendum 2, U-2 finding): the log line is written by Ctx.run_cmd itself (lib/ctx.py), NOT by the calling guard -- guards may perform filesystem side effects ONLY via the three named exceptions in section 1 (tool_discipline's pm-delete-allow consumption, commander's decision log, artifact_hygiene's once-per-session marker), and pr_state / git_discipline are not on that list. Ctx already owns log_error/log_config_error I/O, so routing the timeout log through run_cmd keeps every guard a pure function of (payload, cfg, ctx) while still making a timed-out external call visible in paths.error_log, one line naming the kind, the budget and the argv.
thresholds._note_allowlist_lock_stale_age: How long the pm-delete-allow lock file must sit before it becomes ELIGIBLE for reclaim. Round-16 correction (second pass, after U-1 landed the fix): an earlier version of this note claimed lowering the value "cannot let a live holder be robbed" as if that were a property of the THRESHOLD itself -- the Codex delta review DISPROVED that against the pre-fix code (a lock with no owner record yet, i.e. another process mid-acquisition, used to be treated as stale by age alone, skipping the liveness check entirely, and could hot-spin into an unbounded hang). With U-1's fix, an unowned lock is now NEVER treated as stale, and reclaim requires a CONFIRMED-DEAD recorded owner PID -- so lowering this value now genuinely cannot rob a live holder, but ONLY because reclaim additionally requires that confirmed-dead-PID check, not because of anything this number does on its own. One residual gap the age alone cannot close: if a dead owner's PID is later reused by an unrelated live process, that lock can never be automatically reclaimed regardless of this value -- pm_allowlist.contended_message names the lock file path for that case so a human can remove it by hand.

dependencies._note: ADDED SECTION (psutil addendum item 5). The runtime is stdlib-only EXCEPT for psutil, which the owner adopted so process discovery has one implementation instead of two OS branches. The dependency must be LOUD: it is imported and checked on the DEFAULT deploy path AND by --verify, and a missing module FAILS with a clear message naming the module, the expected version and the recorded install location. A missing C extension that silently turned the two Stop guards into no-ops would be precisely the hollowing-out this port exists to remove — the guards would report 'no orphans' forever and nobody would know.
dependencies._note_check_on_deploy: The check runs on the DEFAULT deploy path, not only --verify. Config validation already refuses to deploy an invalid config (logging.refuse_deploy_on_invalid_config); there is no reason for a missing hard dependency to be treated more leniently than a malformed regex. Deploying a runtime whose process guards cannot function is not a partial success.
dependencies._note_residual_risk: ACCEPTED RESIDUAL RISK, owner-carried. A deploy-time check cannot cover F-20's scenarios BY CONSTRUCTION, because all of them happen AFTER deploy: reinstalling the pinned interpreter, running the hooks as a different user, or a Python minor-version bump each make the user-site psutil disappear without anything re-running install.py. In that state the runtime failure is recorded in dispatch-errors.jsonl — but to the USER it looks identical to a healthy 'no dev orphans', because that is exactly what a Stop guard that cannot enumerate processes reports. There is no in-band signal. Mitigation is procedural, not technical: run install.py --verify after any interpreter change.

required._note_used_by: artifact_hygiene is the OTHER Stop guard but does NOT use psutil — it scans artifact directories, not processes. Only dev_process_hygiene (Stop) and the stop_dev_orphans CLI reach lib/procs.py.
required._note_confinement: psutil is imported ONLY by lib/procs.py, which in turn is imported only by the two Stop-path consumers listed in import_confined_to. NOTHING on the PreToolUse path may import psutil, directly or transitively: PreToolUse runs on every single tool call, and acceptance row 9 caps it at one process — paying a C-extension import there would be a latency regression on the hottest path for a capability it never uses. tests/test_contract.py asserts that no guards/*.py other than dev_process_hygiene.py imports psutil.
required._note_install_scope: USER site-packages, not machine-wide — a common outcome when the machine (system-wide) site-packages is not writeable without elevated privileges, which install_location's shape reflects. It resolves for whichever user actually runs the hooks, but it is a real fragility: reinstalling the pinned interpreter or running the hooks as a different user makes psutil vanish. See CONTRACT.md F-20.

logging._note: ADDED SECTION (justification: acceptance row 8 requires fail-open to stop being silent; the policy must be config, not a literal in dispatch.py). The guard-error destination is paths.error_log (cross-cutting: dispatch.py and lib/ctx.py both write it).
logging._note_fail_open_on_guard_error_removed: A `fail_open_on_guard_error` key lived here and was read by nothing -- dispatch.py's fail-open-on-guard-exception behaviour is not gated by config (see docs/DESIGN.md 'Infrastructure failures block, guard-logic failures fail open'); when any overlay was merged for the dispatch, I-3's BLOCK branch takes precedence. Wiring it would make a guard's runtime error block or allow depending on configuration, i.e. change guard decision logic, which this project deliberately does not offer as a knob. Deleted rather than left dead; do not re-add without also wiring dispatch.py to read it.
logging._note_max_error_log_bytes: The on-disk ceiling for paths.error_log and logging.config_error_log, enforced by lib/io.py:append_jsonl, which KEEPS THE HEAD AND COUNTS THE REST. An entry is appended only while it plus a fixed-width footer still fit under this many bytes; after that nothing is appended and one trailing footer line records how many entries were dropped, rewritten in place per drop. So the file holds the FIRST entries recorded, which is what an investigator needs: when a guard hot-spins (21,612 lines in 25 seconds, observed) the newest entries only say it is still going, while the first ones say what started it. The previous behaviour was truncate-to-empty-then-append, which kept the newest, destroyed the cause, and bounded nothing -- a single entry larger than this value still landed in full. A capped log is FROZEN until someone deletes it (the footer says so); its mtime is the time of the last drop.
logging._note_append_lock_recovery: WHERE THESE LOGS' OWN RECOVERY MESSAGE LIVES, since a reader looking for one here would otherwise find only pm_allowlist.contended_message, which is about the pm-delete-allow LEDGER lock and a different mechanism entirely. Every write to paths.error_log, logging.config_error_log and commander.decision_log is serialised by a per-log append lock (lib/io.py:_locked_append); a writer that cannot take it in time parks its entry, whole, in a `<log>.pending.*` sibling that the next lock holder folds in, so nothing is ever dropped. A lock nobody can be shown to hold is reclaimed automatically -- confirmed-dead owner, unreadable owner record (an interrupted acquire), or simply held past lib/io.py:_APPEND_LOCK_MAX_HOLD_SEC, which is what covers a dead owner's pid having been reused by an unrelated live process. If reclaim nonetheless fails, io.py writes ONE `<log>.STUCK-LOCK.txt` beside the log naming the lock file to delete and where the parked entries are waiting -- there is no config template for that text because io.py is handed a path and bytes and has no cfg to read; it is read by a human in the log directory, never by the model.
logging._note_config_error_log: DISTINCT from guard-error fail-open, deliberately. A guard raising at runtime is an operational event; a config that will not load or a pattern that will not compile is a DEPLOYMENT DEFECT affecting every session until someone fixes it, and burying it in the same stream as transient guard errors is how it stays unnoticed. Entries carry {ts, phase: 'config_load'|'pattern_compile', json_path, guard_scope, error}. install.py validates the config on the default deploy path and REFUSES to deploy an invalid one — catching it at deploy time rather than at hook time is the entire point.

dispatch._note: Absorbed from dispatch-map.json. `tools` is a regex over tool_name anchored as ^(...)$ ; '*' means any. `guards` are module ids resolved to hooks/guards/<id>.py and called in order via their run(payload, cfg, ctx) function IN-PROCESS (no subprocess per guard). First Result with exit_code 2 blocks and its stderr is surfaced. Invariant: at most one guard per chain may emit stdout (today only skill_anchor does).
dispatch._note_stop_hook_active_exempt: J1. Empty today, and it should stay that way. `honour_stop_hook_active_for` and `events.Stop[].guards` are answers to DIFFERENT questions ('which guards honour the flag' vs 'which guards run on Stop') that happen to coincide right now, so they are kept as separate keys rather than one being derived from the other — collapsing them would be a design change, not a port. But 'happens to coincide' plus 'someone adds a third Stop guard' is exactly how a guard quietly stops honouring the flag and reintroduces the infinite Stop loop. So tests/test_contract.py asserts: every id in dispatch.events.Stop[].guards appears in honour_stop_hook_active_for UNLESS it is listed here with a stated reason. Entries are objects: {guard, reason}. Adding a Stop guard therefore either honours the flag or forces someone to write down why not.
dispatch._note_stop_hook_active: LOOP GUARD, and for dev_process_hygiene the ONLY one. Both Stop guards read this boolean from the payload FIRST and return ALLOW immediately when it is true (artifact-hygiene-check.ps1 line 21, dev-process-hygiene-check.ps1 lines 16-17). The harness sets it when the model is already continuing BECAUSE of a Stop hook. Without it: exit 2 -> model continues -> Stop fires -> exit 2 -> forever. artifact_hygiene additionally has a once-per-session marker, but dev_process_hygiene has NO marker at all, so dropping this flag there is an infinite-loop bug, not a missing optimisation. Listed here once rather than as a boolean in each guard section, per single_home_rule. Golden fixture 'QUIET stop_hook_active' must keep passing.
dispatch._note_single_guard_mode_removed: A `single_guard_mode: {enabled, flag}` object lived here and was read by nothing: `--guard` is hardcoded in dispatch.py's argument parser and again in parity.py's invocation, so changing either key would either do nothing or silently desynchronise from that hardcoded call. `dispatch.py --event <E> --guard <id>` still runs EXACTLY ONE guard and returns its Result, skipping the rest of the chain -- required by the parity harness (the old .ps1 side ran one script, so the new side must also run one guard, or a sibling guard in the same chain could decide the result for the wrong reason) and by install.py --verify's smoke check. Deleted rather than left dead; do not re-add without wiring dispatch.py's parser and parity.py to actually read it.
dispatch._note_stdout_emitters: Round-2 review: the declared stdout-emitter set (I-9) was a bare Python string literal ("skill_anchor") inside dispatch.py -- a policy value in code, the exact class this port exists to eliminate. Now HERE, and consumed via cfg at runtime. A second emitter is added by adding its id to this list; adding it only in code would silently discard its stdout instead.

tool_discipline._note_interpreter_delete: 2026-09-06. THE SAME HOLE THE authority-file-in-shell RULE CLOSED FOR THE GRANT FILES, closed here for the general case. Both `detect_pattern` and `segment_start_pattern` were written in terms of SHELL deletion verbs, and an interpreter invoked FROM the shell is a deletion verb neither recognised: an agent blocked on `rm -rf` ran `python -c "import shutil; shutil.rmtree(...)"` and it went through (self-disclosed). The addition is deliberately NOT a ban on interpreters -- the project's own suite runs `python .../run_all.py` constantly and must stay unaffected. THE LINE DRAWN: `detect_pattern` fires only when an interpreter word AND a deletion-API call `name(` appear within 600 characters of each other in the SAME command text; `segment_start_pattern` then requires the delete call in the segment; and the path tokens it yields go through the SAME allowlist, the SAME `..` resolution and the SAME owner pm-delete-allow grant as a shell `rm`. So `shutil.rmtree('C:/owner/x')` blocks, `shutil.rmtree('dist/x')` and `rmtree(.../__pycache__)` do not, and any interpreter command with no deletion call in it is untouched. WHAT FALLS OUTSIDE, stated rather than hidden: (a) `python somescript.py` / `python -m mod`, where the deletion lives in a file and never appears in the command string -- no regex over a command line can see it; (b) a path built from a variable, `os.environ`, `sys.argv` or an encoded literal -- the token check needs a literal path token, so `shutil.rmtree(target)` yields nothing to judge; (c) shelling back out -- `subprocess.run(['rm','-rf',p])` / `os.system('rm -rf ...')` inside a one-liner, which is a generic re-entry past EVERY shell rule (git included), not a delete-specific gap, and wants its own decision rather than being folded in here; (d) a delete call with no parenthesis (`perl -e "unlink $f"`); (e) PIPED deletion -- `find ... | xargs rm -rf`, `echo p | xargs rm` -- where the path is a literal in one segment and the delete verb is in a DIFFERENT one, so no single segment ever holds both and the token check has nothing to judge. (e) is out of reach of a segment-based rule by construction ONLY WHEN THE PATH IS UPSTREAM OF THE PIPE -- corrected 2026-09-06 round 2, because the earlier wording was read as covering `xargs` as such. `xargs` IS in the wrapper list now: when the literal path is an argument in the SAME segment the verb and the path do meet, and both of those spellings block. What remains out of reach is the case where the path is produced upstream, where no single segment holds both. QUOTED SHELL WRAPPERS, 2026-09-06: `bash -c "rm -rf ..."`, `sh -c '...'`, `powershell -Command "Remove-Item -Recurse -Force ..."` and `cmd /c "del ..."` were all ALLOWED -- `detect_pattern`'s first branch had no quote character in its lookbehind class and `segment_start_pattern` required the verb at SEGMENT START, which a wrapper invocation never is. That mattered most for `powershell -Command "Remove-Item ..."`, the native Windows spelling, which the block message names as covered. Closed cheaply, WITHOUT touching segment extraction: `"'` added to the detect class, and a third `segment_start_pattern` alternative requiring a WRAPPER WORD AT SEGMENT START, followed by the verb. The wrapper list is now 19 words (bash|sh|zsh|dash|powershell|pwsh|cmd|sudo|env|exec|xargs|command|nice|nohup|timeout|eval|time|doas|busybox), and what sits between the wrapper and the verb is no longer 'up to 120 non-quote characters' -- that swallowed intervening COMMANDS, so `timeout 10 git rm --cached x` became a false block while the unwrapped form was allowed (round 4). It is an explicit OPTION RUN instead: flags (`-x`, `--long`, `/c`), a flag's single non-flag argument (`sudo -u root`, `xargs -a list.txt`), a bare number (`timeout 5`, `nice -n 10`), and `VAR=value` (`env VAR=1`) -- then an optional quote, an optional run of prefix words, an optional path prefix, and the verb. So the verb must be the FIRST word after the options, which is what keeps `timeout 10 git rm` and `env FOO=1 npm rm` allowed while `timeout 5 rm -rf <path>` and `env VAR=1 rm -rf <path>` block. Both halves of that are false-positive control, and both were reached by trying the looser thing first: a bare quoted verb turned `git commit -m "rm docs/old.md"` and `git commit -m "del old/files"` into blocks, and an UNANCHORED wrapper word turned `git commit -m "sh broke, rm tests/x"` into one -- `bash`, `sh` and `cmd` are ordinary English in a commit message. A rule that blocks routine work gets switched off, and then protects nobody. Anchoring costs nothing real: `x && bash -c "rm ..."` still splits on `&&` into a segment that starts with the wrapper. NOTE a PRE-EXISTING false positive of the same family, not introduced here and not changed here: the FIRST alternative has always matched a segment that starts with a delete verb, so `git commit -m "x; rm docs/old.md"` blocks because `;` is a segment separator. That is the segment-splitter's, and wants the same segment-extraction rework alternative (e) does. Paths inside the wrapper's quotes reach the token check because token_strip_chars already strips `"'`. The goal is to stop the NATURAL spelling of the bypass -- the one an agent reaches for the moment it is blocked -- not to prove evasion impossible; see docs/DESIGN.md 'What owner grants do not guarantee', which says the same thing about the authority-file rule. PREFIXED VERBS, WRAPPER PREFIX WORDS AND `find`, 2026-09-06 (final review, the round after the wrappers above): a fixture sweep found the residue list was reading as exhaustive when it named only the piped case, and seven more spellings measured ALLOWED through the dispatcher -- `sudo rm -rf <path>`, `env rm -rf <path>`, `/usr/bin/rm -rf <path>`, the same three INSIDE a wrapper (`bash -c "sudo rm ..."`, `bash -c "exec rm ..."`, `bash -c "/bin/rm ..."`), and `find <dir> -name x -delete` / `find . -name '*.db' -exec rm {} \;`. By this rule's OWN standard -- a spelling a writer would naturally produce is the rule not working, not residue -- those are defects: they are exactly what an agent reaches for the moment `rm -rf` is refused. THREE ADDITIONS, all of them narrow: (1) an OPTIONAL PATH PREFIX `(?:[^\s;|&()"']*[\\/])?` immediately before the verb, in `detect_pattern`'s first branch and in both verb positions of `segment_start_pattern`, so `/usr/bin/rm` and `/bin/rm` are the verb they are. It cannot widen into a bare word: the prefix must END in a separator, so `git rm docs/old.md` and `cp a/rm b` still do not start a segment with a delete verb (both re-measured). (2) `sudo|env|exec` added to the WRAPPER WORD list, plus `(?:(?:sudo|env|exec|command|nice|nohup|time|doas)\s+)*` (the actual 8-word run in the pattern) after the optional quote, which is what reaches the wrapper form `bash -c "sudo rm ..."` -- the wrapper-word list alone does not, because the verb must follow the quote. `git` is deliberately NOT a prefix word and must never become one: `git rm` is ordinary tracked-file work that git itself records. Anchoring at segment start still does the false-positive control, and the case that proves it (`git commit -m "sudo broke, rm tests/x"`) is pinned beside the three older ones. (3) A `find` BRANCH in both patterns, matching `find ... -delete` and `find ... -exec <verb>` within 300 non-separator characters; `-exec git rm {} \;` does not match it, for the same reason as (1). WHAT (3) COSTS, accepted knowingly and pinned as a fixture: `find . -name '*.pyc' -delete` now BLOCKS, because `.` is a path token outside the allowlist -- the same verdict `rm -rf .` has always had, and the safe direction, but it is a recursive delete rooted at cwd rather than at a disposable directory, so the routine bytecode path stays `rm -rf <dir>/__pycache__`, which is allowed. The SECOND cost of (3) is more common and is disclosed with it: `find`'s `-name` argument is a path-shaped token like any other, so `find dist/ -name '*.map' -delete` blocks on `*.map` even though `dist/` is allowlisted -- measured. Rejecting `*`-leading tokens was considered and dropped: it would allow `rm -rf *.db`, trading a false block for a real hole. The escape hatch is the shell glob, `rm -rf dist/*.map`, which is allowed because the token carries its directory. A DEFECT, NOT NOISE -- this said the opposite until round 4 and was wrong. The prefixed verb (`/usr/bin/rm`) and Windows switches (`/s`, `/q`) are path-shaped tokens, so they were judged as paths: `/usr/bin/rm -rf dist/x` and `cmd /c rd /s /q dist` BLOCKED while the identical delete spelled `rm -rf dist/x` was ALLOWED. That is not a cosmetic message, it is the rule refusing work its own allowlist permits, which is the failure mode this whole rule is organised against. Both are rejected as tokens now: a delete verb with or without a directory prefix, and a single-letter `/x` switch. THE PRICE, which is why it was declined the first time and is accepted now that the cost of not paying it is known: a file whose basename IS a delete verb (`rm -rf tools/rm`) is no longer judged, and neither is a one-character absolute path (`/s`). Both are in the same family as the pre-existing `foo.rm` residue -- a separator-less name that looks like an API call -- and all three are the price of judging paths by their spelling. `find`'s `\;` terminator is still listed as a bad path and that one IS cosmetic. THE WRAPPER SET IS AN ENUMERATION and cannot be completed: any prefix command not on the list passes (`setsid`, `stdbuf -o0`, `watch -n1`, `ionice` all measured rc=0 and are pinned as residue by an ALLOW fixture). Three were added in round 3 (time|doas|busybox) because they are what an agent reaches for next; the next one is always unlisted, and saying so is the point. ALSO ENUMERATED, in the other direction: the VERB set contains two-letter words that are whole commands elsewhere -- `ri` is Ruby's documentation browser and `rd` a directory-removal builtin, so `ri lib/foo.rb` reads a file and is blocked as if it deleted one. Dropping them would open the cmd and PowerShell spellings the set exists for, so it is named rather than fixed. STILL OUT OF REACH after all three, and now stated in docs/DESIGN.md's residue list rather than implied by its absence: the piped case (e) above; a bare name with no separator and no dot (`rm -rf owner-files`), which yields no path-shaped token at all and is PRE-EXISTING, not introduced here -- `find owner-files -delete` inherits it exactly; and quote nesting, which this rule has no notion of -- a delete verb inside a quoted STRING that a wrapper word precedes at segment start is judged as a delete, which is the safe direction and the reason `git commit -m "x; rm docs/old.md"` blocks.
tool_discipline._note_token_reject_api_names: 2026-09-06, and it is the price of splitting tokens on parentheses. `token_split_pattern` gained `()` so `shutil.rmtree('C:/owner/x')` yields the PATH as its own token instead of one unusable blob; that also yields the CALL as a token (`shutil.rmtree`, `.rmSync`, `.unlink`), which contains a dot and would otherwise be reported as a bad path. The third reject entry drops those. It is written with a GENERIC qualifier (`[a-z_]\w*`), not a known-module list, on purpose: `python -c "a=[1,2]; a.remove(1)"` is ordinary work and a module allowlist would block it. PRECISELY WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT BUY, corrected 2026-09-06 round 3 because the earlier wording overclaimed: the reject drops the CALL token, never the ARGUMENT. So a list/set `.remove()` whose argument happens to look like a path -- `python -c "seen.remove('src/x.py')"` -- still yields `src/x.py` as a path token and still BLOCKS. That is the over-block direction and it is left alone: narrowing it would mean knowing which receivers are filesystem objects, which a regex over a command string cannot -- a rule ordinary Python work trips gets switched off, and then protects nobody. RESIDUAL, accepted knowingly: a bare basename that looks like one of these calls -- `rm -rf foo.rm`, `rm -rf foo.remove` -- is now rejected as a token and so no longer blocked. It has to have NO directory separator (`dir/foo.rm` keeps its slash, does not match `^[a-z_]\w*\.`, and still blocks). Deleting a separator-less file whose extension is literally `.rm` is the whole of what was given up to keep every `.remove(` in ordinary Python from becoming a false block.
tool_discipline._note_dotdot_base: M-9(b), PARITY. tool-discipline-guard.ps1 line 75 resolves a token containing '..' with [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($_), which resolves RELATIVE PATHS against the PROCESS's current directory (Environment.CurrentDirectory) — NOT against the payload's `cwd` field, which the guard never consults for this. An earlier draft of CONTRACT.md said ${CWD}; that was wrong. Preserved as process_cwd. NOTE this makes the rule's verdict on a relative '..' path depend on where the hook process happens to be started, which is a latent inconsistency in the master — recorded as F-18, not fixed.
tool_discipline._note_allowed_path_pattern_pycache: 2026-09-06. `__pycache__` and `*.pyc` are ADDED, because the incident that exposed the interpreter hole was an agent whose underlying need was legitimate -- removing regenerable bytecode -- and the only reason it reached for `python -c "shutil.rmtree(...)"` at all was that `rm -rf hooks/__pycache__` was refused. A rule that blocks routine, harmless work manufactures the incentive to route around it, and the routing-around is the actual danger. Bytecode is reproduced by the next import, so it fails the rule's own premise: it is not an owner working file and it is not unrecoverable. WIDENING IS IMPOSSIBLE BY A MERE SUBSTRING: both alternatives are BOUNDED at each end -- `__pycache__` must be a whole path COMPONENT (start-of-string or `/` before, `/` or whitespace or end after), so `src/__pycache__` and `src/__pycache__/x.pyc` match while `src/my__pycache__stuff` and `__pycache__evil/secrets` do not; `.pyc` must END the token (whitespace or end-of-string after), so `x.pyc` matches and `x.pyc.bak` / `notes.pyches` do not. This is a kind:'path' pattern -- N-1 applies, no inline flag, case sensitivity comes from regex.kinds.path.
tool_discipline._note_allowed_path_pattern_case: N-1. The leading (?i) was REMOVED here and must never be re-added. This is a kind:'path' pattern, so its case-sensitivity comes from regex.kinds.path (IGNORECASE on Windows, NONE on POSIX). An inline (?i) OVERRIDES the compile flag, which silently made this pattern case-insensitive on POSIX too — meaning `rm -rf /home/x/Dist` matched the disposable `dist/` alternative and was allowed. That is precisely the hole the path/text split exists to close, and it looked correct on review because the inline flag was legally placed. Windows behaviour is unchanged (the compile flag supplies IGNORECASE there). tests/test_contract.py asserts that NO kind:'path' pattern contains an inline flag group.
tool_discipline._note_allowed_path_pattern: Converted from the PowerShell form '(\\Temp\\claude\\|/Temp/claude/|scratchpad|\.playwright-mcp[\\/]|(^|[\\/\s])dist([\\/\s]|$)|test-results[\\/]|playwright-report[\\/]|\.claude[\\/]state[\\/]|node_modules[\\/]|/dev/null)'. The dual backslash/forward-slash alternatives collapse to forward slash only because lib/paths.py:to_posix() normalises separators BEFORE matching. Effective value is identical on Windows and correct (not case-folded by accident) on POSIX.

pm_allowlist._note_protected: UNCHANGED by the owner-grants round, on purpose: this ledger is path-scoped (the owner lists the exact paths), which is strictly finer than a whole-rule grant, so `grants.never_exempt` refuses the coarse form and this mechanism stays the way to authorise a delete. One thing DID change around it, without touching this code or this file's format: the ledger is now listed in grants.protected, so no agent can write it any more -- which is what it always assumed and never enforced (it lives under ~/.claude/state, which paths.exempt_patterns exempts, so the commander could write its own authorisation and consume it in the same turn). An existing pm-delete-allow file keeps working exactly as before; only the author has to be the owner now.
pm_allowlist.contended_message: (This specific attempt could not complete: the pm-delete-allow ledger was locked by another process and the lock did not clear in time. Your pre-authorisation was NOT consumed -- simply retry the same command. If this persists, the lock file is {lock_path} -- a dead owner whose PID has since been reused by a live process can never be automatically reclaimed, so remove that file by hand if retrying does not resolve it.)

tool_discipline.message:
BLOCKED (tool discipline): deleting files outside disposable locations is not allowed:
  {bad_paths}
Agents may delete only what they created, and only under the session scratchpad,
.playwright-mcp/, dist/, test-results/, playwright-report/, .claude/state/ or any
__pycache__/ directory (bytecode is regenerable, so it is disposable by definition).
This applies to deletion through an INTERPRETER too -- `python -c "shutil.rmtree(...)"`,
`node -e "fs.rmSync(...)"`, `Path(...).unlink()` -- not only to `rm`/`Remove-Item`.
Reaching for one of those after `rm` was refused is routing around the rule, not
complying with it: report the exact paths instead.
The OWNER may pre-authorise exact paths, one per line, in
  ~/.claude/state/pm-delete-allow   (entries are consumed on use, main chain only).
That file has to be written by the owner themselves, from an editor or a terminal
outside this session -- no agent, the commander included, may write it. Say which
exact paths you need and why, and let them add the lines.
Untracked files elsewhere are the owner's working files and cannot be recovered from git.

tool_discipline._note: SELF-GRANT CLOSURE, shell half (guards/grant_files.py is the Write/Edit half; the two together are the whole of it). `grants.protected` names the files that carry the OWNER's permission -- the grant directory, the pm-delete-allow ledger and both overlay files -- and an agent that can write its own permission is not being permitted by anyone. grant_files blocks the Write/Edit tools; this rule blocks the shell, which would otherwise reach the same files through `python -c "open(...)"`, `sed -i`, `cp`, or a redirect, none of which the shell-file-creation rule covers. Matched as a PATH-SHAPED token (a `.claude` directory component followed by the specific name), never as a bare basename: `grep -rn pm-delete-allow hooks/` and `git log -S ulthar-grants` are ordinary work on ULTHAR itself and must not block, while `python -c "open(r'C:\Users\me\.claude\state\ulthar-grants\x','w')"` must. The leading `(?<![\w.])` is a LOOKBEHIND, not a separator class, and that is load-bearing: requiring a `/` or `\` before `.claude` (the first version of this pattern) missed the RELATIVE spelling of the project overlay -- `printf '' > .claude/ulthar-overlay.json`, run in the repo that overlay governs, which is one command for a STANDING disable of any rule and is exactly the obvious next tool call this rule exists to stop. The lookbehind matches at the start of a token or after a separator while still refusing `foo.claude/...`. SEPARATOR RUNS, 2026-09-06: each separator is `[\\/]+` and not `[\\/]`, plus an optional run of `.` segments (`(?:\.[\\/]+)*`). The single-character class matched exactly one separator, so `.claude\\state\\ulthar-grants\\x` -- which is the NATURAL spelling inside a non-raw Python string, i.e. exactly how an agent writes a Windows path in a `python -c` one-liner -- went straight through, as did `.claude//state//ulthar-grants` and `.claude/./state/ulthar-grants`. Measured end-to-end through the dispatcher before and after; tests/test_grants.py::check_authority_path_separator_spellings_all_block builds every spelling from the config values rather than from literals (a literal in a probe would be blocked by this very rule). RESIDUAL, stated rather than hidden. (0) ONE SEPARATOR-FAMILY SPELLING IS STILL OPEN ON THIS HALF, named here rather than left to be found: a `..` segment (`.claude/state/../state/<grants dir>/x`). Win32 resolves it to the same file as the plain spelling; this pattern does not. It stays open because normalising a path INSIDE A COMMAND STRING is a different operation from matching one -- the string need not even be a path on the machine that runs it, and `..` resolution would have to pick a base directory the command may never use. The exposure is narrow: guards/grant_files.py (the Write/Edit half of the same protection) normalises `..` away before comparing, so only a shell command reaches it. The TRAILING-DOT and TRAILING-SPACE components that used to be listed here are NO LONGER OPEN on either half (2026-09-06 round 2): this pattern tolerates a `[. ]*` run before each separator, and lib/paths.py:norm_for_compare strips the same padding, so both spellings are rc=2. (a) a command that assembles the path from pieces or from a variable ($HOME + '/.claude/state/...') is not matched by any regex over the command text, and no amount of widening this pattern changes that; (b) a command that names only the DESTINATION DIRECTORY carries no authority path at all -- `cp tmp/ulthar-overlay.json .claude/`, `tar -xf x.tar -C ~/.claude`, `git apply`, `git checkout <ref>`, `git stash pop`, `git clone` -- so this rule cannot see it. What (b) can still reach is bounded by grants.never_exempt, which is now enforced against overlay `disable` as well as against grant files: a materialised overlay may weaken ordinary rules, and may not switch off the two rules that protect the authority mechanism itself. A materialised GRANT file for an ordinary rule remains reachable that way and is accepted knowingly -- ~/.claude/state is deliberately disposable, so traffic to it cannot be blocked without breaking the state directory's purpose. See docs/DESIGN.md 'What owner grants do not guarantee'. This rule is in grants.never_exempt: a grant that could switch it off would be a grant that authorises writing grants.
tool_discipline.message:
BLOCKED (tool discipline): shell access to ULTHAR's owner-authority files is not allowed.
  ~/.claude/state/ulthar-grants/   (owner grants -- one-shot rule exemptions)
  ~/.claude/state/pm-delete-allow  (owner pre-authorised delete paths)
  ~/.claude/ulthar-overlay.json, <repo>/.claude/ulthar-overlay.json (rule overrides)
These files are how the OWNER permits something a guard blocks, so no agent -- the
commander included -- may create or change them: an agent that writes its own
permission is not being permitted by anyone. Ask the owner to write the file
themselves, from an editor or a terminal outside this session, and say exactly which
file and which one line.
(Reading ULTHAR's own source that merely MENTIONS these names is unaffected -- this
rule matches a .claude path, not the bare word.)

command_rules._note_dev_server_empty: The config-generalisation round. This shipped a rule requiring a Node heap flag on one specific package.json script name -- that script only exists in one project's package.json; a stranger's repo has no matching script at all, so the rule was permanently dead weight for them (and would misfire the moment THEY happened to name a script that too). Moved to examples/user-overlay.example.json as a generalised example of the same shape. Shipping this list empty is the mechanism-visible-but-inert instance: guards/dev_server.py, its regex_require rule TYPE and its message-formatting stay fully implemented and exercised by tests/fixtures/dev_server (which now inject the example rule via cfg override -- see test_dev_server.py); only the ONE concrete rule instance moved out. This path is overlay-appendable (overlays.project_allowed_paths), so restoring it, or adding an equivalent rule for a different script name, is a one-file edit outside this skill.

git_policy._note: Consumed by guards.git_discipline and guards.pr_state. `global_option_prefix` is the ONE authoritative `-C|-c|--git-dir|--work-tree|--exec-path` prefix regex (lib/gitcmd.py); it is the UNION of the two divergent copies in git-discipline-guard.ps1 (had --exec-path, no quoted-arg support) and pr-state-guard.ps1 (had quoted-arg support, no --exec-path). See CONTRACT.md 'Parity exceptions'.
git_policy._note_deploy_refs_empty: The config-generalisation round. This shipped preview-branch names as universal defaults -- they were ONE owner's convention for their own hosting provider's preview branches, and the deploy_ref_message named that same provider's build specifically. Neither is a fact about git or about ULTHAR; they are this owner's convention. Moved to examples/user-overlay.example.json (see overlays.project_allowed_paths -- this path is overlay-appendable, so a user or project restores or extends it without editing this shipped config). Shipping it empty is the mechanism-visible-but-inert instance the round asked for: the guard, the message template and the phase-order slot all still exist and still fire the moment an overlay populates this list.
git_policy._note_phase_order_pe18: PE-18 (2026-09-05). Two phases added, neither ported from any .ps1 master -- the operating rules said not to bypass hooks/signing and treated force-push as dangerous, but they lived only in prose files nothing ever loaded, so none of it was enforced (confirmed dead before AND after the cutover). `hook_bypass` sits right after `destroyers`, still ahead of `is_write_subcommand`: like blanket_staging/destroyers it is an operation-TYPE check (does this command carry a bypass flag at all) that must not depend on the write-subcommand gate having already matched, even though in practice --no-verify/--no-gpg-sign only ever appear on commit/push (which the gate would pass anyway) -- the placement keeps the same 'operation-type before destination-specific' precedent destroyers already set, rather than a coincidence of which subcommands happen to carry the flag today. `force_push` sits right after `is_write_subcommand` (it needs 'push' context, unlike hook_bypass, so it cannot run before the gate) but BEFORE `deploy_refs`/`protected_push` -- deliberately, so 'you are force-pushing at all' (an operation-type fact) is reported before 'to this specific destination' (deploy ref / protected branch), the same precedence destroyers already has over the branch-specific checks below it. Concretely this changes the message (never the exit code) for `git push --force` while standing on main (golden fixture git-golden-block-force-on-main: was 'you are on the protected branch', now the force-push message) and flips `git push --force-with-lease` on a feature branch from ALLOW to BLOCK (golden fixture git-golden-pass-force-on-feature, renamed to git-golden-block-force-with-lease-on-feature) -- both now parity:false citing PE-18, since the .ps1 masters have no such rule and cannot agree.
git_policy._note_phase_match_target_null: R-c. `match_target: null` on the current_branch phase means 'this phase matches NOTHING — it shells out to git rev-parse'. It does NOT mean 'unspecified, use the default'. Do not write `phase.get('match_target') or 'probe_quotes'`: that would hand a probe string to a phase that has no pattern to match, and the null is the signal that this phase leaves regex-land entirely. null and 'probe_quotes' are different states, not a value and its fallback.
git_policy._note_phase_match_target: S-7. match_target is DATA on each phase, not prose. git_command_detect is the sole raw-matching phase (it runs before $probe is built at git-discipline-guard.ps1 line 28); current_branch matches nothing (it shells out to git rev-parse). Encoding it per phase removes the standing risk that a creator applies the section-level default uniformly and quietly makes `git commit -m "drop the -a flag"` start blocking, or makes the detect phase miss a command whose quoted text was blanked.
git_policy._note_phase_order: EXPLICIT evaluation order for git_discipline, ported top-to-bottom from git-discipline-guard.ps1 (detect line 23, G1 lines 34-53, G3 lines 55-77, isWrite line 80, G4 lines 83-100, G2 lines 102-113, rev-parse lines 115-132) -- PLUS two 2026-09-05 additions with no .ps1 line to cite, `hook_bypass` and `force_push`; see `_note_phase_order_pe18` for where each sits and why. The order is load-bearing: `git clean` while standing on main must yield the DESTROYER message, not the protected-branch message, because destroyers are checked before the branch is ever resolved. `is_write_subcommand` is an early ALLOW gate — a command that is not commit/push/merge/rebase returns 0 without git being run at all, which is why read-only git commands cost nothing.
git_policy._note_match_target: Per-phase match_target now lives on each phase_order element (S-7). Summary: git_command_detect matches RAW (line 23, before $probe exists); every other matching phase uses the QUOTE-STRIPPED probe built once at git-discipline-guard.ps1 line 28 — which is exactly what keeps `git commit -m "drop the -a flag"` and `git commit -m "merge main later"` passing (both golden fixtures). See git_policy.pr_state.match_target for that guard's separate, all-raw behaviour.
git_policy.blanket_staging_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): blanket staging via {why} is not allowed.
Stage an EXPLICIT file list instead, so an unexpected file cannot ride along:
  git -C <repo> add path/to/file1 path/to/file2
  git -C <repo> commit -m "<why this change was needed>"
If a file you did not expect shows up in `git status`, stop and report it rather than
staging everything.
git_policy.destroyers_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): {why} is not allowed.
Untracked and modified files in the working tree belong to the owner and may be
unrecoverable. If a deliberate reset/restore is required, report it and let the owner
run it. (Read-only git commands are unaffected.)

hook_bypass.why: -n (short alias of --no-verify on commit; skips pre-commit/commit-msg hooks)

git_policy._note_hook_bypass_short_n: PE-18. `-n` is `git commit`'s documented short alias for `--no-verify` (on `git push`, `-n` means `--dry-run` instead, an unrelated and harmless flag -- this entry deliberately targets `commit\b` only, never `push`). Matched as a combined-short-flag CLUSTER (`-(?!-)[A-Za-z]*n[A-Za-z]*`), the same shape `blanket_staging`'s `commit-a-short` entry already uses for `-a` -- so `git commit -na`, `git commit -an`, and `git commit -n` are all caught, consistent with that existing precedent (accepted there for `-am` already). A rule whose one-letter alias walks straight through it is the exact class of gap this task exists to close.
git_policy._note_hook_bypass_no_signoff: PE-18. `--no-signoff` was considered and deliberately left OUT: it omits a DCO trailer, not a hook run or a cryptographic signature -- a different risk class from the two principles files' and the harness's own standing rule, neither of which ever names it. Folding it into the same list under the same message ('hooks and signing exist to catch problems') would misdescribe what it actually does. Adding it needs its own message, which nothing here asked for.
git_policy._note_hook_bypass_gpgsign_config: PE-18. `-c commit.gpgsign=false` (an equivalent signing bypass) is deliberately OUT OF SCOPE here, for a structural reason, not an oversight: `-c KEY=VALUE` is consumed by `global_option_prefix` BEFORE any suffix ever sees the command text (it strips `-c commit.gpgsign=false` as a leading global option, exactly the way it strips `-c user.name=x`), so a `hook_bypass` suffix entry for it would never fire -- catching it needs a RAW-target check ahead of the prefix, the same class of change `git_command_detect` required. That is a real, separately-scoped gap; flagged for the owner rather than folded in silently.
git_policy.hook_bypass_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): {why} is not allowed.
Hooks and commit signing exist to catch problems before they leave the working tree;
skipping them is a per-instance human decision, never a default an agent reaches for
itself. If a hook is genuinely broken, fix the hook -- or report it and let the owner
decide to bypass it themselves. (Read-only git commands are unaffected.)
git_policy._note_force_push_short_f_cluster: PE-18. `-f` is matched as a combined-short-flag CLUSTER (`-(?!-)[A-Za-z]*f[A-Za-z]*`), not just a bare `-f` token -- `git push -uf` / `-fu` / `-vf` are all valid git invocations that still force-push, and no other `git push` short option uses the letter `f` for anything else, so widening from an exact `-f` match to the cluster shape (the same precedent `blanket_staging`'s `-a` entry already sets) closes a one-letter combining bypass instead of leaving it as an unexamined gap.
git_policy._note_force_push_lease: PE-18. `--force-with-lease` is materially safer than `--force` (it refuses if the remote ref moved since your last fetch, so it cannot silently clobber a collaborator's unseen push) but it is NOT split into a separate, unblocked rule here -- danger.md itself listed `git push --force` / `--force-with-lease` side by side as needing per-instance owner approval, and this guard has only two outcomes, ALLOW or BLOCK (no third 'warn but proceed' primitive exists in a PreToolUse hook) -- there is no way to 'warn' short of blocking. The actual harm being guarded against is an agent unilaterally rewriting PUBLISHED history at all, not just the clobber-someone-else's-commit case --force-with-lease narrows; that harm is identical for both flags. The message says so and names --force-with-lease as the flag to request when the owner does authorize a force-push.
git_policy.force_push_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): {why} is not allowed.
Force-pushing rewrites history that other people or CI may already be building on.
--force-with-lease is safer than --force (it refuses if the remote moved since your
last fetch) but still overwrites the remote ref without the owner's say-so. If a
force-push is genuinely required, report it and let the owner run it themselves,
preferring the lease-checked form:
  ! git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>
(Read-only git commands are unaffected.)
git_policy.deploy_ref_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): pushing to the deploy branch '{ref}' is reserved for the owner.
Each push triggers a production deployment; agents never decide that.
Report the branch/commit that is ready and let the owner run:
  ! git push origin <branch>:{ref}
git_policy.protected_push_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): pushing to the protected branch '{ref}' is not allowed.
Work on a feature branch and open a PR:
  git -C <repo> switch -c feature/<name>
  git -C <repo> push -u origin feature/<name>
git_policy.protected_branch_message:
BLOCKED (git discipline): you are on the protected branch '{branch}'.
Never commit, push, merge or rebase directly on it -- branch first, then PR:
  git -C <repo> switch -c feature/<name>
Then re-run this command. (Read-only git commands are unaffected.)

pr_state._note_match_target: S-7. pr_state matches the RAW command in EVERY phase — pr-state-guard.ps1 never builds a quote-stripped probe. This is a real asymmetry with git_discipline (which probes from line 28 onward); it is preserved, not harmonised, and stated as data so a creator cannot infer git_discipline's default applies here. Consequence to be aware of: a commit message containing the word 'push' can influence pr_state's parsing in a way it cannot influence git_discipline's.
pr_state._note_push_detect_suffix: N-2. This is a SUFFIX, composed by the guard as git_policy.global_option_prefix + suffix — exactly the way blanket_staging[].suffix and destroyers[].suffix are composed. It previously held the full prefix alternation inline, which duplicated global_option_prefix byte for byte: a mirror value, the thing section 3.2's single-home rule calls a review blocker. The concrete risk was not theoretical — adding a new global option such as --bare to global_option_prefix would have left this copy untouched and silently reopened the very bypass PE-4 closed. There is now exactly ONE place where the git global-option alternation is defined.
pr_state._note_tokenisation: Ported from pr-state-guard.ps1 lines 33-40, with the parsing patterns moved out of the guard and into config. Algorithm: split the raw command on push_split_pattern and keep part[1]; cut it at the first segment_split_pattern delimiter; split on token_split_pattern; drop empties and tokens matching token_reject_pattern (flags); then take tokens[refspec_token_index]. NOTE: index 1 is the FIRST refspec after the remote name, NOT the last one — the master's own comment says 'last <remote> <src>[:<dst>] pair', and that comment is WRONG about its own code. Preserved as-is for parity; recorded as a Finding (F-14) rather than fixed. If that token contains ':', keep the part after it (the destination); then strip refs_heads_strip_pattern.
pr_state.message:
BLOCKED (PR state): branch '{branch}' has no OPEN pull request -- every PR on it is already merged or closed:
{pr_list}

A push here is silently lost (nothing will merge it). Instead:
  1. git fetch origin && cut a NEW integration branch from origin/main
  2. merge the pending branches into it, push, and open a NEW PR (one PR per batch)
Rule: check `gh pr view <n> --json state` BEFORE pushing to any branch that had a PR.

brief_rules._note: Consumed by guards.brief_gate (PreToolUse Agent/SendMessage). Evaluation: detect -> classify kind (first matching `match`, else the kind whose match is '*') -> run that kind's rules IN ARRAY ORDER; the FIRST failing rule blocks. Array order IS evaluation order, matching brief-gate-guard.ps1's top-to-bottom flow (gate 4/5 first because forwarder/committer kinds return early; then gate 1, 2b, 2, 6, 3 for creator briefs).
brief_rules._note_compact_header: PE-19 (2026-09-05). A creator dispatch previously had to carry FOUR separate hand-written markers to pass gates 1/2/3/6 (an APPROVAL:<file>.md reference, a STATE/acceptance-table mention, an OWNER-CONFIRMED: block, and -- when UI-shaped -- a design-skill/no-ui declaration). The compact header `BRIEF: <file>.md | <kind> | no-ui` (kind and the no-ui tag both optional) replaces that, WITHOUT weakening any gate: (1) detect.brief_pattern gained a line-anchored alternative recognising the header shape itself as brief-shaped text; (2) each of forwarder/committer/reviewer's `match` gained a `| <kind>` alternative so the header alone classifies the brief (creator has no alternative to add -- it is the '*' fallback, so a header naming any other recognised kind classifies as that kind, and everything else, including `| creator` or no kind token at all, falls through to creator exactly as before); (3) gate6's `reference_pattern` now accepts `BRIEF:` as well as `APPROVAL:`, so the SAME file resolution gate6 already performed (existence + age-or-OWNER-OK) also resolves the compact form -- no new file format, no new trust boundary; (4) gate1 and gate3 (both `require_pattern`) may now ALSO be satisfied by the content of THAT SAME resolved file (see guards/brief_gate.py `_resolve_reference_text`) -- so the acceptance-table and owner-decision detail can live in the approval file (which the creator already had to write and the owner already had to read, per gate 6's own protocol) instead of being restated inline; (5) design_cases' ui-design-skill case gained one satisfied_by alternative, `\|\s*no-ui\b`, so the header's own `| no-ui` tag can stand in for naming a design skill -- but ONLY that literal tag; it is evaluated by design_cases exactly as before (content-triggered, no file fallback), so a brief that actually contains UI-trigger words still blocks unless it either names a real design skill or carries `| no-ui` -- claiming `| ui` (or any other tag) does not bypass it. The long form (separate APPROVAL:/STATE mention/OWNER-CONFIRMED:/design-skill markers) keeps working unchanged; nothing was removed, only alternatives were added. See references/briefing-templates.md -> compact header for the worked example, and STATE.md for the acceptance evidence.

detect._note_brief_pattern_compact: The final alternative recognises the compact header ITSELF as brief-shaped text, line-anchored (scoped `(?m:...)`) and requiring the full `BRIEF: <name>.md |` shape -- not a bare `BRIEF\s*:` -- specifically so an ordinary long dispatch that happens to contain the prose 'in brief: ...' cannot be misrouted into creator-gate enforcement (M-11 already warns that widening this pattern affects EVERY gate).

kinds._note_content_match: PRECEDENCE (2026-09-06). Alternatives 1-2 are HEADER forms; alternative 3 classifies BY CONTENT (`codex exec` / `Delta re-review` / `Final delta` -- tokens a forwarder dispatch deliberately carries). The leading negative lookahead is NOT a classification lock: it encodes the precedence rule *a brief that labels its own kind is that kind*, so the content route only ever applies to UNLABELLED text. It excludes every bracket kind header AND any `APPROVAL:<f>.md` / `BRIEF:<f>.md` reference (gate 6 lives only on `creator`, so such a reference is a creator marker -- its PRESENCE is creator precedence, never forwarder/committer evidence). Without it, array position beat the label: `[Creator Brief] ... Final delta ...` classified forwarder, whose only rule is gate 4, skipping creator gates 1/2/3/6. Regression: test_brief_gate.py::test_kind_precedence_over_content_signals, case creator-label-beats-forwarder-content-route (inline rather than in fixtures/briefs/ because tests/parity.py pins the total fixture-file case count and that file was outside the scope of this change).

kinds.match: (?i)\[Committer Brief|BRIEF\s*:\s*[\w.\-]+\.md\s*\|\s*committer\b|\A(?![\s\S]*(?:\[(?:Creator|Investigator|Forwarder|Committer|Reviewer|Fallback Reviewer|Auditor)\s+Brief|(?:APPROVAL|BRIEF)\s*:\s*[\w.\-]+\.md))(?=[\s\S]*(?m:^\s*Files\s*:))(?=[\s\S]*(?:をコミット|コミット依頼))(?=[\s\S]*(?:Stage\s+exactly\s+these\s+files|をステージ|未ステージ))
kinds._note_content_match: 2026-09-05 owner-reported false positive; 2026-09-06 REWRITTEN after a HIGH review finding. Alternatives 1-2 are HEADER-ONLY (bracket form, compact header). A Japanese commit dispatch -- the owner writes briefs in Japanese -- carries neither, so it fell through to the '*' creator fallback and design_cases' ui-design-skill case fired on its UI vocabulary, demanding a design skill from a dispatch that by nature invokes none. Alternative 3 classifies BY CONTENT and is a conjunction of three POSITIVE locks plus one precedence lookahead. The asymmetry runs one way: a committer misread as creator only annoys, while a creator misread as committer SKIPS gates 1/2/3/6 -- so every lock must be something the author of a COMMIT dispatch deliberately writes, never something a creator brief merely lacks. LOCK 1, a LINE-ANCHORED `Files:` header -- stricter than gate5's own `Files\s*:|Files \(`, on purpose: gate5 is a contract check AFTER classification and may be permissive, the classifier is the trust-relevant step; prose like 'edit these files (see plan)' must not qualify. LOCK 2, a commit-AS-THE-TASK phrase: `をコミット` (the object particle, i.e. 'commit <this>') or `コミット依頼` -- never a bare verb, since a creator brief routinely says 'commit when the tests pass'. `Commit\s+Brief` was REMOVED from this lock on 2026-09-06: references/briefing-templates.md:498 puts the words 'Commit Brief' inside the CREATOR round template (コミットは PM の指示後に Commit Brief で haiku へ), so a template-following creator brief satisfied it for free while a template-following commit dispatch never says it. LOCK 3, the STAGING DISCIPLINE the Commit Brief protocol mandates and gate5's own message spells out ('staged from an enumerated per-file list only; state what must remain unstaged'): `Stage exactly these files` (references/briefing-templates.md:424, the template's own line), `をステージ` ('stage <these>'), or `未ステージ` ('unstaged'). This REPLACES the previous third lock, 'no APPROVAL:/BRIEF: reference anywhere', which was a HIGH finding: it identified a committer dispatch by the ABSENCE of a creator requirement, so a creator brief that FORGOT its mandatory approval -- exactly what the gates exist to catch -- classified committer and returned ALLOW. Absence of a requirement is never positive identification. `ステージ` appears NOWHERE in the creator/STATE templates, and lock 3 deliberately avoids any `add -A` signal: the creator template's own 禁止 list (briefing-templates.md:506) contains `git add -A`, so an add-based signal would be boilerplate-matched. PRECEDENCE (the leading negative lookahead) is NOT a fourth lock: it encodes the rule *a brief that labels its own kind is that kind*, so the content route applies only to UNLABELLED text. It excludes every bracket kind header and any `APPROVAL:<f>.md` / `BRIEF:<f>.md` reference -- gate 6 lives only on `creator`, so such a reference is a creator marker and its PRESENCE is creator precedence (the one thing the old rule got right, kept, reframed). It does not depend on kinds[] array order, which is why it also protects `[Reviewer Brief]`/`[Auditor Brief]`: the reviewer kind sits AFTER committer in the array, so before this lookahead a labelled reviewer brief carrying the locks would have classified committer. MECHANICS: `[\s\S]*` not `.*` (kind 'text' is IGNORECASE only, never DOTALL); `\A` so search evaluates the lookaheads once rather than at every offset; no `\b` beside kana (kana are \w, so the boundary would not be where it looks). Alternatives 1-2 are unaffected by the exclusion: a bracket or compact header anywhere in the text is matched by them at that offset, while alternative 3 only ever runs at offset 0. RESIDUAL, stated rather than hidden: an UNLABELLED brief carrying a line-anchored `Files:` header AND `をコミット` AND a staging-discipline phrase is classified committer even if it was meant as creator work. The creator template uses `File scope:`/`Do NOT edit:`, never `Files:`, never any staging instruction, and commits are routed through a separate dispatch. Gate 5 (explicit file list) is UNCHANGED and still runs for every committer brief -- lock 1 makes it harder to REACH this kind, never optional once here.

commander._note: ADDED SECTION (justification: commander-guard's activation modes, marker lookup order and message were hardcoded; they are policy, and the exempt list they share with skill_anchor already had to move to paths.exempt_patterns).
commander._note_marker: First existing path wins (repo override, then global default). The mode is the FIRST LINE only, trimmed and casefolded.
commander._note_max_decision_log_bytes: OWN key, deliberately NOT logging.max_error_log_bytes, even though it ships the same 2 MiB value today. paths.error_log / logging.config_error_log only grow when something is wrong; decision_log grows on every main-chain Write/Edit the guard evaluates, in NORMAL operation -- a different failure mode needs a knob an operator can tune independently, even if nobody has yet. It also uses a DIFFERENT cap function (lib/io.py:append_jsonl_drop_oldest, not append_jsonl): the error logs keep the HEAD (an investigator wants what STARTED a hot-spin) and freeze once capped; a decision-log reader wants the opposite -- 'did commander just block me, and why' is always a question about the newest entries -- so this cap drops whole lines from the FRONT to make room for each new one instead of freezing. No footer, no drop counter: a dropped decision is just an old decision, not a diagnosable fault the way a dropped error-log entry is.
commander._note_default_mode_when_unrecognised: J2. This is a MODE ID (a key of `modes`), not a mode token. The guard resolves it as modes[default_mode_when_unrecognised] -> 'observe'. It previously held the literal 'observe', duplicating modes.log_only: renaming the vocabulary would have left the fallback pointing at a token that no longer existed, and the guard would have silently fallen through to a mode nobody chose — the same failure class as F-21. Effective behaviour is unchanged: an unrecognised marker value still means observe (log, never block).
commander._note_tools_named: N-4. Resolves from regex.named_alternations and is anchored by this guard as ^(...)$ — the literal it replaced was a third copy of the same list.
commander._note_empty_file_path_behaviour: PARITY, and it is a real divergence between the three Write/Edit guards — preserved, NOT harmonised. commander-guard.ps1 reads tool_input.file_path only; for NotebookEdit the harness supplies `notebook_path` instead, so $file is empty. The empty string matches no exempt pattern, and line 91's outside-cwd exemption is skipped precisely because the path IS blank (`-not [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($file)`), so exempt stays false and the guard BLOCKS every NotebookEdit under enforce mode. deploy-guard.ps1 line 15 and skill-anchor.ps1 line 69 both take the opposite branch and exit 0 on a blank path. Three guards, three behaviours, from the same missing field. Do not fix unasked — see F-16.
