grants._note: OWNER GRANTS -- the generalisation of the delete rule's pm_allowlist to every rule any guard enforces. A grant is ONE EMPTY FILE, created by the OWNER, whose path under `dir` IS the rule identifier: <dir>/<dotted config path>/<rule id>, e.g. ~/.claude/state/ulthar-grants/git_policy.force_push/push-force. That is the SAME addressing the overlay `disable` operation uses (overlays._note_disable), deliberately -- one syntax, two lifetimes: an overlay `disable` is STANDING and scoped to a repository (or to the user's own machine, in the user overlay); a grant is scoped to this machine and CONSUMED THE FIRST TIME IT IS USED. If you want a rule off permanently, that is not a grant, it is a `disable` in your user overlay -- and saying so is the whole reason no session-scoped or standing grant exists here. Consulted by a guard at the moment it would BLOCK: it takes the file (see `_note_claim` for what decides the winner of a race -- NOT os.remove, which was measured double-succeeding on Windows) and lets that ONE call through, then the next identical call blocks again. `main_chain_only` is not negotiable per-grant: a grant never applies to a subagent whatever it names. Every consumption is logged to `log` with the rule id and what it permitted; a grant that was never used is observable as the file still sitting there.
grants._note_self_grant: THE POINT OF `protected`, and the reason this section exists at all rather than just a second copy of pm_allowlist. The owner's words are 'when the USER has permitted it'. A grant file that the AGENT can create does not establish that -- it is the agent permitting itself, which is what repeatedly happened with pm-delete-allow (it lives under ~/.claude/state, which paths.exempt_patterns exempts, so the commander could Write it and then consume it in the same turn). On a single-user machine the author of a file cannot be authenticated, so the answer has to be structural: every file that carries the owner's permission is UNWRITABLE BY EVERY AGENT, commander included -- guards/grant_files.py blocks the Write/Edit tools, command_rules.tool_discipline/authority-file-in-shell blocks the shell. WHAT THIS DOES NOT GUARANTEE is written out in docs/DESIGN.md and is not hidden here: it does not authenticate anyone, and an agent that assembles the path from pieces in a shell command, or that persuades the owner to run a command they do not understand, still gets through. What it removes is the OBVIOUS path -- self-granting now requires deliberate evasion rather than being the natural next tool call. Visibility was considered as an alternative and rejected: a log line is written after the file is already deleted and the force-push already pushed, so it can only tell the owner what was done to them, never let them decide.
grants._note_claim: WHO WINS A RACE for one grant. The obvious answer -- 'os.remove is atomic, so only one of two racing tool calls can consume the file' -- is FALSE on Windows, and it was measured before it shipped rather than assumed: two threads racing os.remove() on the same path, 300 trials, BOTH reported success in 144 of them (48%); see tests/test_grants.py::check_consume_primitive_is_exactly_one_winner. Same class of Windows surprise recorded for os.replace in guards/tool_discipline.py:_reclaim_stale_lock, and it would have meant two concurrent calls both granted by ONE grant file about half the time they raced -- the double-spend a ledger lock exists to prevent, reintroduced by the design that was supposed to need no lock. The winner is therefore decided by `os.open(<grant><claim_suffix>, O_CREAT|O_EXCL)` -- exactly one winner in 300/300 trials in the same harness -- and only the claim winner removes the grant. `claim_stale_sec` bounds the one residue: a marker outlives its creator only if that process died mid-consume (microseconds), and without a reclaim that residue would make one identifier silently ungrantable forever -- validate() cannot report a stray marker as an error, because a marker legitimately exists during any other process's consume.
grants._note_log: OWN key, like commander.max_decision_log_bytes: this log grows only when a grant is actually used, and an operator asking 'what did my grant let through' wants the record intact, so it uses lib/io.py:append_jsonl (keep the head, freeze at the cap with a drop counter) rather than the decision log's drop-oldest. `permitted_truncate` bounds the one payload-derived field -- the command or file path the grant permitted -- so a pathological command cannot fill the cap on its own. That field is deliberate: an audit line saying only WHICH rule was exempted, and not what it let happen, is not an audit line.
grants._note_never_exempt: Rules that neither a grant NOR an overlay `disable` may switch off; a grant file or an overlay entry naming one is refused loudly at dispatch time, exactly like one naming a rule that does not exist. THE OVERLAY HALF WAS MISSING UNTIL 2026-09-06 (lib/ctx.py:_refuse_never_exempt): `command_rules.tool_discipline` is in overlays.project_allowed_paths, so a cloned repo could switch off `authority-file-in-shell` PERMANENTLY by shipping one overlay file -- the same power a grant is refused, with a longer lifetime. Both arguments below are about the RULE, not about the lifetime, so they apply verbatim. ENFORCED ON BOTH LAYERS, the user's own overlay included: this rule matches a command that NAMES the file, so `cp x ~/.claude/` or `tar -xf -C ~/.claude` (destination directory only) materialises a user overlay exactly as easily as a project one -- 'it is the owner's own file' is not a structural property here. THIS LIST IS ITSELF PINNED: it is not in overlays.list_merge, so it merged by REPLACEMENT, and the user layer has no path restriction -- `{"grants": {"never_exempt": []}}` in a user overlay would have handed back both the disable route and the grant route (lib/grant.py:validate reads the MERGED cfg). An overlay that changes it is refused loudly. The owner's way to switch these two off is `enabled: false` in THIS file, which no overlay can reach. The owner's standing decision that a project overlay may weaken ORDINARY rules is untouched. `authority-file-in-shell` is here because a grant that switched it off would be a grant that authorises writing grants -- the mechanism would close over itself. `delete-outside-disposable` is here for a different reason: a whole-rule one-shot on it is strictly COARSER than the pm_allowlist grant that rule already has (any path in that one command, instead of the exact paths the owner listed), and the path scoping is the entire reason that mechanism exists -- so the delete rule keeps its own, unchanged, and this one refuses the blunt form. NOTE the Write/Edit half of the protection (guards/grant_files.py) needs no entry here: it is not a rule in a config rule list, so it has no identifier a grant could name -- it is unaddressable by construction.

overlays._note: The config-generalisation round. ADDED SECTION -- the plugin layer for policy this round exists to build. ULTHAR ships the mechanism (this section, plus lib/ctx.py:merge_overlays) and universal rules (everything else in this file); WHOSE rules an individual json path holds comes from OUTSIDE ulthar, via the two files named below. Consumed once per dispatch, in dispatch.py's main(), immediately after load_config() and inside its OWN try/except -- a bad overlay is treated exactly like a bad config.json (BLOCK, exit 2, logged to logging.config_error_log, never a silent per-guard fail-open), but it gets its own recovery text (dispatch.infra_recovery.overlay), because 'redeploy the master' is the wrong instruction for a file that is neither under hooks/ nor in git. A malformed overlay ENTRY is caught in TWO places, and the split is the point. (1) At merge time the merge refuses any entry whose shape it can DERIVE -- a declared list's element schema, a section merged with a section, an undeclared list replaced with the wrong element shape (see _note_project_allowed_paths (2)). (2) Shape is structure only, so a STRUCTURALLY VALID entry with a semantically wrong VALUE still reaches its guard -- a tool_discipline append carrying `target: "bogus"` passes every merge check and then KeyErrors inside the guard. That one is caught by its CONSEQUENCE instead: while ANY overlay is merged, a guard that raises BLOCKS and names the overlay file rather than being turned into ALLOW by the dispatcher's fail-open (dispatch.py:_attribute_to_project_overlay). So the claim is not 'no guard is ever handed content it cannot handle' -- it is that no such content can end as a SILENT allow. This is deliberate: an overlay that silently degraded to 'ignored' on error would be exactly the hollowing-out this whole project exists to remove — a rule nobody can see is gone.
overlays._note_paths: TWO layers. `user_path` (under the user's OWN ~/.claude) is as trusted as this file -- the user owns both -- so it is deep-merged with no ALLOWLIST restriction: it may add, replace or remove anything at any declared path EXCEPT the four sections named in `pinned_paths` below (dispatch, grants, regex, overlays), and subject to the container rule that a rule LIST may only be merged with a list and a section only with a section. Those two bounds are not about trusting the owner less: they are the difference between a file the owner wrote and a file an agent materialised there with `cp`/`tar -C`/`git clone`, which the shell rule cannot see because it names no path. Everything else is the same as editing this file directly would be, and it gets the same explicit `disable` operation. `project_path` (inside the repo the agent is working in, resolved against the PAYLOAD's cwd, expanded via lib/paths.expand exactly like every other ${CWD}-rooted path in this config) states the REPO's policy, and that policy wins while you work in that repo: it may add rules at `project_allowed_paths` and may `disable` named rules there, including rules that were protecting you. That is deliberate (see `_note` and `_note_project_allowed_paths`). It is bounded in two ways only, neither of which second-guesses the repo's policy. (a) SCOPE: `project_allowed_paths` lists the RULE lists; the rest of this file is ULTHAR's own wiring (paths.python_exe, dispatch.events, logging.*, overlays.*), and a cloned repo repointing the interpreter the hooks run under, or the log they write to, is not policy at all -- it is the repo rewriting the guards that judge it. (b) SHAPE: an entry appended to a declared list must have the shape that list's existing entries have (a scalar list is homogeneous; an append_by_id entry carries at least the keys every existing entry carries, with the same types), and a violation is refused at merge time naming the OFFENDING FILE and the offending dotted path. (b) binds the user layer too, as a correctness check rather than as a boundary: a wrong type there is always a typo, never a policy.
overlays._note_absent: Absent is the common case and must stay cheap and silent: both paths are checked with a single os.stat() each: a missing file is not an error, produces no log line, and costs one failed stat() call on the hot PreToolUse path -- negligible next to load_config's own os.stat()+open() on config.json itself, and no json.load() is attempted for a file that is not there.

list_merge._note: Per-JSON-path merge strategy AND element shape for every path an overlay may touch, so 'append vs replace' and 'what a valid entry looks like' are both DATA, not something a creator infers from the field's shape. A value is either a bare strategy string (the element shape is then DERIVED from the entries this file already ships at that path) or an object {"strategy": ..., plus a declared shape}, which is what a list that ships EMPTY needs -- there is nothing there to derive from. 'append': the value at this path must be a list of PLAIN scalars (strings/ints); overlay items are appended after the base list, in layer order (base, then user, then project), and an item ALREADY PRESENT (by `==` equality) is a silent no-op, not a duplicate -- an overlay restating an existing entry is not an error, it is just redundant. TYPE RULE, and it applies to the USER layer too: an 'append' list is HOMOGENEOUS, and an item whose type differs from the type the base list already holds -- or, for a list that ships empty, from the declared `element` -- is a ConfigError naming the overlay file and the dotted path (lib/ctx.py:_check_scalar_conforms). Putting the string '8080' into `dev_processes.ports`, which holds ints, is refused at load, by install.py at deploy time and by the dispatcher at the next tool call; so is the integer 5 in `git_policy.deploy_refs`, which git_discipline feeds to re.escape(). Either used to merge silently and then never match anything, or raise inside a guard and be converted to ALLOW by the fail-open. This is a deliberate BEHAVIOUR CHANGE to the fully-trusted user layer, made because a wrong type there is always a typo and never a policy. 'append_by_id': the value must be a list of OBJECTS each carrying an `id` key (exactly the shape command_rules.tool_discipline/dev_server, git_policy.destroyers/blanket_staging/hook_bypass/force_push and design_cases.cases already use); overlay items are appended the same way, but an overlay item whose `id` MATCHES an id already present at that path (from the base config OR an earlier-merged user layer) is REFUSED: an id identifies a rule and must stay unique, so a redefinition is ambiguous rather than forbidden. To switch the existing rule off, say so explicitly with the top-level `disable` list (see _note_disable) and give any replacement entry its own id. SHAPE RULE for append_by_id: an appended entry must carry at least the keys EVERY existing entry at that path carries, and for each of those keys a value of the same type, wherever the existing entries agree on one (lib/ctx.py:_object_schema). The existing entries ARE the schema, so it cannot drift from this file as this file grows -- unlike a hand-written required-key table, which is the objection that made validation look unattractive the first time. EMPTY BASE LISTS -- the case with no entries to derive from -- are not waved through: an append to a list that ships empty and declares no shape is REFUSED outright, naming the path, the overlay file and what to declare. The two paths that ship empty are exactly the two documented extension points (git_policy.deploy_refs, command_rules.dev_server) and both declare their shape below, so the shipped examples/user-overlay.example.json and examples/project-overlay.example.json still merge. A new empty list added here without a declared shape is un-appendable rather than un-validated: refusal is the safe default, and the error says exactly what to add. Every path here is one this file itself declares as a list at that exact location; a mismatch (overlay supplies a list where cfg has a dict, or vice versa) is also a ConfigError.

git_policy.deploy_refs._note: Ships EMPTY (the owner-specific preview-branch names moved to examples/user-overlay.example.json), so the element type is DECLARED here rather than derived from entries that no longer exist. guards/git_discipline.py feeds each entry to re.escape(), which raises TypeError on a non-string -- a guard crash, hence a fail-open, and exactly the bypass that treating an empty base list as 'accepts anything' allowed.

command_rules.dev_server._note: Ships EMPTY and is THE documented extension point users are expected to use, so it must stay appendable -- hence a declared required-key list rather than the refusal an undeclared empty list gets. These are exactly the keys guards/dev_server.py reads for its one rule type (regex_require); an entry missing any of them raises inside the guard. Adding a second rule type there means revisiting this list, which is the standing cost of the one path that cannot derive its own schema.

pinned_paths.why: it decides which guards are ROUTED at all, so emptying one event's list switches every guard on that event off without disabling anything
it is the owner-authority mechanism itself -- which files no agent may write, which rules nothing may exempt, where a grant lives, and the message text a guard formats
it holds the named alternations guard routing resolves through and the per-platform compile flags, so a rewrite unroutes or defangs a guard without naming it
it is the merge mechanism, this list included -- an overlay able to rewrite it would have every path on it for free

overlays._note_pinned_paths: 2026-09-06, final review round 2. The SUBTREES no overlay may change, in EITHER layer -- enforced by lib/ctx.py:_refuse_pinned_paths against a REWRITE (base subtree value vs merged subtree value) and against a `disable` whose left half IS a pinned prefix or starts with '<prefix>.' (a disable removes an entry from any dotted list and runs AFTER the merge, so a value comparison alone would not see it). Read from the BASE cfg, so an overlay cannot empty the list on its way past; `overlays` being one of the four is what pins this list itself. WHY SUBTREES AND NOT A LIST OF LEAVES. Round 1 pinned four leaves (dispatch.events, grants.protected, grants.never_exempt, overlays.pinned_paths). The review then measured FIVE more single-overlay switch-offs that the leaf list did not reach, every one of them rc=0 on a Write of a grant file that is rc=2 with no overlay: {"disable":["dispatch.events.PreToolUse/None"]} (a CHILD path -- entries carry no id, so _entry_id yields the string 'None' and the whole chain is removed); {"regex":{"named_alternations":{"write_edit_tools":"__never__"}}} (the Write/Edit chain routes through that name, so nothing runs); {"grants":{"enabled":false}} (guards/grant_files.py returns ALLOW immediately, so all four protected files become writable INCLUDING the user overlay, which makes it permanent); {"grants":{"dir":"..."}} (the Write half follows grants.dir while this file's authority-file-in-shell pattern holds the literal, so a repointed directory was reachable through the shell and the grant was honoured end-to-end); and {"grants":{"protected_message":5}} (grant_files formats it with .replace(), so a non-string is an AttributeError -> the dispatcher's fail-open -> ALLOW). Enumerating leaves is chasing instances of a class. The class is: a path that is NOT A RULE but decides what a rule can do. Those live in exactly four sections, and pinning the section closes the ones nobody has thought of yet -- including the scalar-type case, which shape validation does not cover (it validates LIST entries; every scalar a guard reads with a type assumption is the same shape of bug). THE ARGUMENT for pinning the user layer at all is unchanged and is about materialisation rather than trust: `cp x ~/.claude/`, `tar -xf -C ~/.claude`, `git apply`, `git clone` all reach the user overlay without naming it, so 'it is the owner's own file' is not a structural property. WHAT AN OWNER LOSES, stated because it is more than round 1 took: from an overlay they can no longer reroute guards, re-list the protected files, change either carve-out, move the grant directory, turn the grant mechanism off, or EXTEND regex.named_alternations (adding a new edit-style tool name is a legitimate use and it is now refused from an overlay -- the owner's call to revisit, not a bug). WHAT THEY KEEP: all six in THIS file, which no overlay can reach and which install.py re-registers the hooks from. Everything outside the four sections stays overlayable, logging.* and paths.* included, and every RULE list stays appendable and disableable from both layers -- the owner's standing decision that a project overlay may weaken ordinary rules is untouched. ONE CONSEQUENCE WORTH NAMING: authority-file-in-shell's pattern holds the literal `ulthar-grants` rather than deriving it from grants.dir. Deriving would be new machinery (regex.named_alternations is for *_named REFERENCES at routing and guard sites, not for interpolation inside a rule's pattern), and it is no longer needed: grants.dir is inside the pinned `grants` subtree, so the literal cannot drift away from it.
overlays._note_project_allowed_paths: The RULE PATHS, and therefore the line between project policy and ULTHAR's own wiring. It is no longer a non-weakening boundary -- a project overlay may switch rules off here (see `_note_disable`), which is the owner's decision and the model this file now describes. What it still does is say WHICH json paths hold rules a project has any business having an opinion about. A path not in this list -- logging.max_error_log_bytes, thresholds, paths.python_exe, dispatch.events, deploy_guard, overlays.* -- is refused with ConfigError naming it, for both an append and a `disable`. The reason is the tool's own integrity, not doubt about the repo's policy: those keys decide which interpreter the hooks run under, which guards are routed at all, where the evidence is written, and whether the deployed runtime can be edited from inside a cloned repo. A repo setting them is not stating a policy about its own development, it is rewriting the guards that judge it -- and deploy_guard in particular protects the deployed copy of every guard, so disabling it from inside a repo would let that repo replace the whole mechanism, including this restriction. Everything a repo can actually express about how work is done in it is a rule at one of these paths, and every one of them is both appendable and disableable -- including command_rules.tool_discipline/delete-outside-disposable and git_policy.destroyers/*, which are the rules that protect untracked files. WHAT IS STILL GUARANTEED, and it is now about ACCIDENTS rather than about permission: (a) merge-time SHAPE VALIDATION (lib/ctx.py:_merge_list, _object_schema, _check_scalar_conforms) refuses an entry whose shape the consuming guard could not read, so no guard is ever handed content it will crash on and the dispatcher's fail-open cannot be used to remove a guard wholesale; the schema is DERIVED from this file's own entries at that path, so it cannot drift as this file grows, and a list that ships empty declares its shape beside its strategy in `list_merge`. (b) a `disable` naming nothing existing is refused, so a typo cannot leave the author believing a rule is off when it is on, or the reverse. (c) every overlay failure names the overlay FILE it came from whatever the underlying exception type (lib/ctx.py:_merge_layer), because the recovery text tells the reader to delete that file and must never point at nothing. (d) guard-time source attribution (dispatch.py:_attribute_to_project_overlay) remains as the backstop for the case shape validation cannot reach -- a structurally valid entry whose VALUE is wrong for the consuming guard (`target: "bogus"`, whose `probes[target]` raises KeyError). It BLOCKS naming the overlay file instead of failing open. It is not a boundary and must not be re-promoted to one; the guard is NEVER re-run (an earlier design did, and a marker file vanishing between the two runs made an innocent overlay look guilty and locked the operator out -- documented at length in dispatch.py:_attribute_to_project_overlay). WHAT IS NOT GUARANTEED, stated plainly: a project overlay CAN leave you with fewer rules than your own config gives you, and can cause a DENIAL (a repo shipping a broken overlay blocks tool calls in that repo, loudly, with its own path in the message). The first is the policy; the second is the failure mode, and both are visible.
overlays._note_disable: HOW A RULE IS SWITCHED OFF, and the only way it can be. TWO RULES ARE EXCLUDED FROM IT ENTIRELY: everything named in grants.never_exempt is refused here as well as to a grant file, from BOTH layers -- see lib/ctx.py:_refuse_never_exempt and grants._note_never_exempt for the argument, which is that those rules are not policy about a repository, they are what decides what a repository may do. An overlay (either layer) may carry a top-level `disable` key: a list of "<dotted config path>/<rule id>" strings, e.g. {"disable": ["git_policy.destroyers/clean", "git_policy.force_push/push-force"]}. The left half is exactly the dotted path used by `list_merge` and `project_allowed_paths`; the right half is the entry's `id` for an object list, or the scalar itself for a plain list ("git_policy.protected_branches/main"). A dotted path never contains '/', so the FIRST '/' splits it, and a ref-shaped id ("release/1.0") stays addressable. Implemented in lib/ctx.py:_collect_disables/_apply_disables: the named entry is REMOVED from its list after every layer has merged, so exactly one rule stops applying and every sibling entry in the same list -- and every other rule in the same guard -- keeps enforcing. That blast radius is the whole point: what this operation replaces is a malformed entry crashing a guard, which removed everything that guard enforced, silently. FAILURE IS LOUD: an identifier that matches no rule (a typo, or a rule that has since been renamed) is a ConfigError naming the overlay file, the path and the ids that ARE there -- a `disable` that silently switched nothing off would be the same invisible failure. So is a malformed identifier, and, for a PROJECT overlay, one naming a path outside `project_allowed_paths`. Every one of those is checkable without running a guard. VISIBILITY: when a PROJECT overlay disables anything, dispatch.py logs it to logging.config_error_log (phase `overlay_disable`, with the overlay path and the ids) and states it in the operator's context. Both fire on FIRST ENCOUNTER -- the first dispatch of the session that sees those disables, whatever event it is -- and then not again for that session and that set of ids. They were gated on `event == "SessionStart"` until 2026-09-06, which meant a session that started outside the repository and later entered it, or one whose overlay appeared after startup, honoured the disables from the very next tool call while recording them nowhere and saying nothing, with no later SessionStart guaranteed -- the silent removal this model was rebuilt to prevent, mechanism changed and invisibility intact. The CADENCE is what must not change: printing on every tool call would train the reader to ignore the notice and would push real entries out of a size-capped log. "Once" therefore lives on disk (dispatch.py:_overlay_notice_marker -- a digest of session id + overlay path + disabled ids, under paths.logs_dir/overlay-notice, expiring after a day), beside the logs deliberately: the marker is unwritable exactly when the log write is, and when it cannot be recorded the notice REPEATS rather than disappearing. The context notice rides the same JSON envelope skill_anchor uses (raw text only on skill_anchor.plain_stdout_events) and is attached only when no guard in the chain emitted stdout itself, since a second emitter would corrupt the first one's envelope.
overlays.example_note: Two worked examples ship as documentation, never as live defaults: examples/user-overlay.example.json (the two former shipped offenders -- git_policy.deploy_refs and command_rules.dev_server -- restored as a USER overlay) and examples/project-overlay.example.json (a project adding a restriction of its own AND disabling one of ULTHAR's by id -- the two things a project overlay may do). Copy the relevant one to overlays.user_path / overlays.project_path and edit.
